analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC crack down on telecom robocalls and scams.
analysis.headline: The robocall-enforcement bill never got a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill removes a decades-old law that shields telephone and cable companies from FTC enforcement. With that shield gone, the FTC could sue or fine phone carriers over illegal robocalls and spam scams. It never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who gets illegal robocalls and spam calls — essentially all phone users. The FTC could go after carriers whose networks are used to deliver scam calls, and consumers could get more FTC enforcement against telecom companies generally.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, common carriers (phone companies) are regulated exclusively by the FCC and are exempt from FTC regulation; the bill removes that exemption and subjects common carriers to FTC regulation.

The bill's stated findings are that illegal robocalls and spam calls are a growing problem and that exemptions in the FTC Act limit the FTC's enforcement capabilities against illegal robocalling and spam calling.
It preserves FCC and state authority to protect net neutrality and consumers, so it adds FTC enforcement without displacing the FCC's rules.

analysis.who_pays: Telecommunications companies would face a second federal regulator (the FTC) and potential enforcement actions and penalties over robocalls and other practices.

drawbacks.text: Doubling regulators can create conflicting rules: telecoms could face inconsistent FCC and FTC requirements over the same conduct, which companies argued made compliance harder.
FTC enforcement against robocalls is reactive — it acts after scams reach consumers — so the bill would not by itself block calls before they arrive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real but modest: robocalls are pervasive and FTC authority is a proven enforcement tool, yet the bill alone would not stop calls before they ring. The cost is a regulatory change affecting a few dozen large carriers. On balance the consumer benefit outweighs the compliance cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 28, 2018, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action followed; the bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phone and cable companies benefit: they remain exempt from FTC regulation and were never subject to a robocall-enforcement law.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; never held a hearing or markup before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans supported it.

industries.note: Common carriers are currently exempt from FTC regulation and would lose that shield, gaining a second enforcer with fining power. Consumers would gain FTC pressure on robocalls and spam delivered over these networks.
